title: Matot: clear before all (Numbers 32:22)
hook: be "clear before the LORD, and before Israel": innocent, and seen to be fair

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses asked two tribes, shall your brothers go to war while you sit here, and they chose to cross over. Your line was don't sit it out. Who did you show up for? Day four hundred seventy-five.

The treasurer of the parents' association who suddenly has a new car. Maybe it was an inheritance. Maybe a raise. It's probably fine. But people talk, and once they start, it's hard to stop them. Being honest and looking honest aren't quite the same thing. Moses knew it. As he finishes the deal with Reuben and Gad, he adds a phrase that sounds like legal fine print. The rabbis turned it into a very practical rule for daily life.
screen: `THE TREASURER'S NEW CAR.` → `HONEST, AND LOOKING HONEST.` → `A PHRASE LIKE FINE PRINT.`

segments.voice: Moses tells the two tribes: if you cross over and fight until the land is subdued, and then come back, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "ye shall be clear before the LORD, and before Israel." Clear before God, and also before the people. In Hebrew, nekiyim, clean, innocent. It isn't enough that God knows you kept your promise. The other tribes have to be able to see it too. The rabbis built a whole way of living on that small phrase, and before Israel. In the Mishnah, tractate Shekalim, the person who went into the Temple treasury chamber to take out coins wasn't allowed to wear a garment with a hem, or shoes, or tefillin, or an amulet. Anywhere a coin might hide. Why? In case he became poor, people would say it was a punishment for stealing; and in case he became rich, people would say he'd taken it from the chamber. Then the Mishnah quotes our verse: a person must be clear before people, just as before God. The Talmud tells of two priestly families with secret skills. One family baked the special bread for the Temple. Its children were never seen eating fine bread, so no one could suspect the family of taking any. The other family made the Temple incense. Its brides never wore perfume, for the same reason. That's a lot to give up. They did it so their honesty would be visible, not just real. The point isn't image management. It's that trust is something the whole community shares, and you protect it by leaving nothing to suspect.
screen: `NEKIYIM: CLEAR BEFORE GOD AND ISRAEL.` · `NO HEM, NO POCKET, NO SHOES.` · `NO FINE BREAD, NO PERFUME.` · `TRUST IS SHARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be open about one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that's perfectly fine but might look odd from outside: money you handle for others, a decision you made quietly, a friendship someone might misread, time you spent that no one knows about. Ask yourself: is there anything here I could make clearer, simply by saying it out loud? Choose one thing you could be open about this week, not out of guilt, but to keep trust easy. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Matot. The portion where Moses tells two tribes to be clear before the Lord and before Israel: honest, and seen to be.
Your line: clear before god and people. Today, if you handle something on someone else's behalf, tell them plainly how it went. Day four hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: The principle drawn from Numbers 32:22, being clear before people as before God, guides Jewish practice in handling communal funds, and the Mishnah's rules for the Temple treasury are still taught as its classic example.

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall be clear, innocent (Numbers 32:22).

trapdoor: what you thought: legal fine print in a land deal.
what it means: be honest, and also leave nothing for others to suspect.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Shekalim 3:2 cites Numbers 32:22 for the treasury rules; Yoma 38a praises the houses of Garmu and Avtinas for their visible honesty.

notes: Numbers 32:22 JPS 1917: '...then ye shall be clear before the LORD, and before Israel'; confirm (KJV has 'guiltless').
Mishnah Shekalim 3:2: no bordered cloak, shoes, tefillin or amulet; cites Numbers 32:22 and Proverbs 3:4. Confirm details.
Yoma 38a (and Tosefta Yoma 2:5–6): House of Garmu (showbread) and House of Avtinas (incense); confirm.
